new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alalaw 'how cold!'. In Tarma and the dialect of northern Junin word-final stress can occur as a result of the elision of a final syllable. [p. 206] ... In Pacaraos Quechua (see section 3.2.9) stress is phonemic. It may lie either on the penultimate or on the final syllable. ... Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo [p. 207]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's penultimate pattern (penultimate stress), stated for Quechua in general rather than Ayacucho specifically, and adding the interjection/emphatic word-final exception; the Ayacucho grammar sketch (pp. 208-232 per the index) returned no stress fragment under any query, so nothing there contradicts the general rule. The archive.org copy is controlled-lending ( could not be reached by automated download); the text was reconstructed from full-text-search highlight fragments, so the quoted passage has one gap between examples (34) and (35) marked in the copy consulted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word (the general Quechua rule, stated for 'most Quechua dialects'); word-final stress only in interjections and emphatic expressions, plus dialect-specific deviations that do not include Ayacucho.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the fragments retrieved.
new_statements.exceptions: Interjections and emphatic expressions can carry word-final stress (alalaw 'how cold!'). Deviant systems are named for other varieties only: Tarma/northern Junín (final stress from elision of a final syllable), Pacaraos (phonemic final vs penultimate stress, first-person -´y), quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo (word-initial and syllable-structure-dependent stress), QIIA Ferreñafe, QIIB Amazonas, and the sixteenth-century coastal dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken's stress statement is made for 'most Quechua dialects' in the family-level phonology section (§3.2.5), not in the Ayacucho sketch; Ayacucho Quechua (QIIC, departments of Ayacucho and Huancavelica) is not among the varieties they list as deviant, so the general penultimate rule applies to it. Burns & Alcócer 1964 is a Huamanga (Ayacucho) teaching text in Spanish for Ayacucho Quechua [quy] per the SIL record.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding 1963 quotation is verbatim at the stated page (p. 8) in the copy downloaded now, and the 1964 corroborating quotation is verbatim in the copy consulted (section 2.3, pp. 6-7). A third held source (Zariquiey & Cordova 2008:34) independently gives the same rule with suffix-shifting paradigms. The classification fixed penultimate (penultimate stress, domain word) matches all three; the only deviations the sources mention are final stress as an emphatic morpheme / a small set of marked exceptions, which the record already notes via the StressTyp exceptional-word entries. Weakness is only that the deciding citation is a 1963 audio-lingual course rather than the reference grammar: the record's grade field is empty and the cite should be promoted to Sola & Parker 1964 section 2.3 (held) plus Zariquiey & Cordova 2008 section 3 p. 34 (held), with Parker 1969 ch. 1 (paywalled, DOI 10.1515

sources.note: Live URL is 404 on http/https (retried with a browser User-Agent); the Internet Archive /web/2/ redirects to a 2026 capture of the 404 page; the availability API gave capture 20220705192710, which delivered the 22-page PDF with a text. It is the manual for the LLAMA language-aptitude test battery (Swansea); its stimuli are 'a Central American language' and 'a British Columbian Indian language'; Quechua is never mentioned. The Glottolog/catalog link of this work to Ayacucho Quechua is a misattribution; nothing here bears on word stress in any Quechua variety.
